item.title: Gemini 4 Neon has caught up to Opus 5.5, but almost no one noticed the release
item.description:
A week ago, I would have laughed in the face of anyone who said I'd be praising Google's neural network. The market had long since shrunk to Opus 5.5 at the top and endless arguments with ChatGPT at the bottom. And then Gemini 4 Neon came out: a "mid-tier" model that understands tasks with half a word, fixes bugs in others' MCP adapters itself, and finds server performance bottlenecks that have been sought for three weeks. I'll tell you why there's silence around the release, what Google just fixed in the Antigravity cache, and where Neon's weak spots lie. See tests and numbers

item.title: What's Happening to the Developer Profession: My Experience and Industry Data
item.description:
How it started with us. I work in a development team of about twenty people: 1C developers and related stacks, several testers, and analysts. This text is not theory, but what my colleagues and I have gone through ourselves in recent months while preparing an AI implementation plan for the next few years. It all started without any plan. In the spring of 2026, part of the team was already playing with AI agents in personal projects – just out of interest. In the summer, it turned into a work practice: manual code writing by developers decreased significantly, but the load on code reviews and architectural decisions increased sharply – exactly the shift in focus that all analysts are now talking about. By the end of the summer, we began experimenting with local generation on our own hardware and created a common knowledge base – first for all the stacks we worked with, and then a separate base for 1C and related technologies was выделена from it. We launched regular internal meetings to share experiences with AI tools – once a week, it would have been difficult to keep pace without them. In the fall, we connected a cloud AI agent (in compliance with data processing requirements) as the main work tool for the entire team, and before that, we cleaned the code of credentials and other sensitive information to work safely with cloud agents. Separately, we started a pilot of spec-driven development (SDD) – first with analysts and developers, and stumbled upon the industry benchmarking project PRISM, which we began to use to verify the models' advertising claims on our own tasks, rather than taking their word for it. There is also a less pleasant finding: part of the team noted a deterioration in sleep and general well-being due to the sharp immersion in new technology. I think it's honest to talk about this – acceleration rarely comes for free, and this should be factored into the implementation pace, not hushed up. Read more

item.title: If you look into the depths for a long time
item.description:
I am creating a companion program for Euro Truck Simulator 2 - a radio called "Channel 15". Ideally, it's a radio play where the player is one of the viewers, as well as actors and directors, and eighteen fictional drivers drive around the map, talk on the radio, remember past conversations, and eventually start to recognize you. It's not a mod, it doesn't touch game files, it works alongside the game and reads telemetry. In this article, I don't want to talk about how it's built inside (that's been done), but about what I've hit a wall with now. I'm worried that my characters are flat. And I can't decide if they need depth at all. I'm figuring this out in writing because I've been going in circles in my office alone for a week. Read more

item.title: Stop Learning Every Unfamiliar Word. How to Learn to Read in English
item.description:
About eight years ago, I decided to combine two useful things: to delve deeper into JavaScript and improve my English at the same time. I found a technical book in its original language, opened the first chapter, and started reading. Dozens of words were added to my dictionary in an evening, and I barely made any progress in the book. It turned out that I was simultaneously learning programming, translating from English, and trying to memorize a bunch of new words. And I didn't enjoy any of these activities. Read more

item.title: Where I Spent My Yandex Grant: Writing a C++/CUDA Engine for LLMs from Scratch That Outperforms llama.cpp on an Old RTX 2080 Ti
item.description:
In early 2026, Yandex announced a grant for the best open-source projects on their new SourceCraft platform. I submitted my project, np — a C++ analog of NumPy with CUDA support and manual SIMD optimizations (AVX2/AVX-512), which outperforms the original by 2-20x in speed and uses 1.5x less memory (I detailed this with benchmarks in my previous article 'Speeding Up and Optimizing NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, and Scikit-learn'). At the time, I had just started exploring 'vibecoding' and used it to achieve this level of optimization. To my surprise, I saw my project in the list of winners. Honestly, I was very surprised and initially didn't believe it: I had never received any grants for projects before and didn't quite understand what the program committee found so appealing about my repository. It seemed like nothing particularly outstanding. Nevertheless, 600,000 rubles appeared in my account. The logical question arose: how to spend it? According to the contest rules, grants are given to projects with a clear development plan. The organizers saw this future – unlike me, for which I am very grateful. I, on the other hand, wasn't entirely sure where to go next. Rewrite the entire NumPy in C++ using vibecoding? Possible, but why? I experimented with some functions and realized I had already solved the basic acceleration task. Where I spent the grant

item.title: Trust, but Verify — or How to Limit AI Agent Permissions at Different Levels
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My AGENTS.md clearly states: 'do not work in main' and 'force push only with permission.' I analyzed 193 git push calls from my sessions: in about a third of cases, the agent didn't ask for permission, thrice it pushed directly to main, and out of 31 force pushes, I only allowed two. And git is relatively harmless – the same agent accesses databases, S3, and Kubernetes with my credentials, and one day it might execute DROP DATABASE. Hooks, sandboxes, and roles have been discussed on Habr before; I will break down security mechanisms in agent development into four levels: what each actually protects, how to configure it, and where its boundaries lie. The agent actively accesses all your services and systems under your accounts and with developer privileges – how can you protect your infrastructure from non-deterministic agents and reduce potential negative impacts? Defend against Skynet.

item.title: How to Choose Platforms for Brand Mentions in AI Responses — I Scoured a Study from Ahrefs
item.description:
I recently saw a study from Ahrefs: brands with ten times more mentions on web pages have about 3.7 times more mentions in AI responses — significantly less than one might expect from such a difference. When choosing platforms for brand mentions, it's important to consider that Ahrefs only studied third-party pages with search traffic. The persuasiveness of the link to AI responses is also important: the authors compared different companies, so the coefficient itself does not justify purchasing publications. Read more
